challenges.title: Subsets
challenges.prompt:
Given a list of **distinct** integers `nums`, return every possible subset of it (the power set), including the empty subset and the whole list.

No subset may appear twice. You may return the subsets in any order, and the numbers inside each subset in any order.

examples.explain: Each of the 3 numbers is either in or out, so there are 2^3 = 8 subsets.

constraints: All values in nums are distinct
hints: Each number is either in a subset or not: two choices per number, so 2^n subsets in total.
Backtrack with a start index. Record a copy of the path at every call, then for each i from start onward: append nums[i], recurse with i + 1, pop.
Record a copy of the path (path[:] in Python, [...path] in JavaScript), not the path list itself, or every entry ends up empty.
challenges.explanation: Backtracking over a take-or-skip decision tree. Every call records a copy of the current path, then extends it with each later item in turn and undoes the choice afterwards, so each subset is built exactly once, in increasing index order. An iterative alternative starts from [[]] and, for each number, adds a copy of every existing subset with that number appended.

challenges.title: Permutations
challenges.prompt:
Given a list of **distinct** integers `nums`, return every possible ordering (permutation) of all its values.

You may return the permutations in any order.

examples.explain: 3 choices for the first slot, 2 for the second, 1 for the last: 3! = 6.

constraints: All values in nums are distinct
hints: Order matters here, so a start index is not enough: any value not used yet can fill the next slot.
Keep a used array (or a set). In the loop, skip used values; otherwise mark it, append it, recurse, then pop it and unmark it.
Record a copy of the path when its length equals the length of nums.

solution.python:
def permute(nums):
    result, path = [], []
    used = [False] * len(nums)

    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return result

challenges.explanation: Backtracking where every unused value is a candidate for the next position. A used array tracks which values are already in the path; both the path and the used flag are undone after each recursive call. Complete paths of length n are copied into the result. Swapping values in place is an equally good alternative that avoids the used array.

challenges.title: Combination Sum
challenges.prompt:
Given a list of **distinct** positive integers `candidates` and a positive integer `target`, return every unique combination of candidates that adds up to `target`. Each candidate may be used **any number of times**.

Two combinations are the same if they use each value the same number of times, so `[2, 2, 3]` and `[3, 2, 2]` count as one. Return the combinations in any order, with the values inside each in any order. If nothing works, return an empty list.
hints: Use a start index so each combination is only built in one order. That is what stops [3, 2, 2] from repeating [2, 2, 3].
After choosing candidates[i], recurse with the same i (not i + 1) so it can be picked again. Record the path when the remaining target is 0.
Sort the candidates first; then you can break out of the loop as soon as a candidate is bigger than what remains.
challenges.explanation: Backtracking with a start index and reuse. Sorting lets the loop stop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target, because all later candidates are larger. Recursing with i (not i + 1) allows the same value again, and never moving back below i keeps each combination in nondecreasing order, so no combination is produced twice.

complexity.time: O(n^(T/m + 1)) in the worst case, for target T and smallest candidate m
complexity.space: O(T/m) for the recursion and the path

challenges.title: Generate Parentheses
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer `n`, return every string of `n` opening and `n` closing parentheses that is **balanced**: reading left to right, the number of `)` never exceeds the number of `(`, and the totals are equal at the end.

Return the strings in any order.
hints: Build the string one character at a time and keep counts of how many ( and ) you have used.
You may add ( while opened < n, and ) only while closed < opened. Any other prefix can never become balanced.
When the string reaches length 2n it is complete: add it to the result.
challenges.explanation: Backtracking with two pruning rules instead of generating all 2^(2n) strings and filtering. An opening parenthesis is allowed while fewer than n are used, and a closing one only while it has an unmatched opening parenthesis to close. Every branch that survives these rules ends in a valid string, so no work is wasted on dead ends. The JavaScript version passes new strings down, so it needs no un-choose step.

challenges.title: Word Search
challenges.prompt:
Given a grid of letters `board` and a string `word`, return `true` if the word can be spelled by a path of cells, starting anywhere and moving one step up, down, left or right at a time. A cell may be used at most once in the same path.

Return `True` or `False` in Python.

examples.explain: C (row 0) to A (row 0) to R (row 1, middle) to S (row 1, right).
The only C would have to be used twice.

constraints: board and word contain only English letters
hints: Try every cell as a starting point and run a depth-first search that matches one letter per step.
dfs(r, c, k) fails if (r, c) is off the grid or board[r][c] differs from word[k], and succeeds once k reaches the word length. Otherwise try the four neighbors with k + 1.
Mark the cell (for example with '#') before exploring its neighbors and put the letter back afterwards, so a failed path does not block a later one.
challenges.explanation: Depth-first backtracking from every starting cell. Each step must match the next letter; the current cell is marked with '#' while it is on the path (the mismatch test then rejects it automatically) and restored afterwards, so other paths can use it. The search stops at the first complete match.

complexity.time: O(R * C * 3^L) for an R x C board and a word of length L

challenges.title: Phone Keypad Letter Combinations
challenges.prompt: On a phone keypad each digit from 2 to 9 stands for some letters: 2 = abc, 3 = def, 4 = ghi, 5 = jkl, 6 = mno, 7 = pqrs, 8 = tuv, 9 = wxyz. Given a string `digits`, return every string you can spell by picking one letter for each digit, in any order. If `digits` is empty, return an empty list.

examples.explain: Three choices for 2 times three choices for 3 gives 9 strings.

hints: Build the string one digit at a time. At position i you choose one of that digit's letters, then move on to position i + 1.
Write a recursive helper that takes the index and the letters chosen so far. When the index reaches the end, add the finished string to the answer.
Handle the empty input up front: without that check, the recursion would add one empty string.
challenges.explanation: This is the plainest backtracking shape: one decision per position, each with a few options, and a complete answer at the bottom of the recursion. The choose, explore, undo rhythm reuses one path list instead of copying strings at every level. There are up to 4^n results of length n, so the output size dominates the running time. An iterative version that extends a list of partial strings digit by digit is equally good.
